subject: zoology
question_text: Compare and contrast cartilaginous and bony fishes.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.37, SAQ 31). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. BOOK WORDING: the book lists 'cycloid, ctenoid, ganoid or cosmoid' scales for bony fishes. Cosmoid scales are found in the extinct lobe-finned fishes and in lungfishes, not in the common bony fishes of the syllabus, so the card gives cycloid, ctenoid or ganoid. The book also prints 'Scolidon' and 'Exocoetus'; the accepted spellings are Scoliodon and Exocoetus.

steps.label: Habitat, skeleton, mouth
steps.margin_note: Write this as two columns or as paired lines. Keep the same order in every row.
lines: Bony fishes live in all aquatic habitats, both
In cartilaginous fishes it is made of cartilage.
In bony fishes it is made of bone.
The mouth is ventral in cartilaginous fishes.
The mouth is terminal in bony fishes.
steps.why: The name of each group already gives the skeleton, so the skeleton row is written first and every other row is then read as a consequence of a cartilage or a bone body.
common_mistakes: Writing that cartilaginous fishes have bones as well. Their skeleton is cartilage throughout life.
Giving a terminal mouth to a shark. The shark mouth opens on the under side, so it is ventral.
steps.memory_tip: Cartilage body, mouth underneath. Bone body, mouth at the front end.

steps.label: Scales and air bladder
steps.margin_note: Two rows here. The air bladder row carries the reason as well, so give it a line.

steps.why: The missing air bladder is why a shark sinks when it stops swimming, so this row explains a behaviour and not only a structure.
common_mistakes: Giving cycloid scales to the shark. Placoid scales belong to cartilaginous fishes only.
Writing that both groups have an air bladder. It is absent in cartilaginous fishes.
steps.memory_tip: No air bladder, so a shark must keep swimming. A bony fish can hang still in the water.

steps.label: Excretion and caudal fin
steps.margin_note: Two more rows. Add the meaning of hetero and homo in brackets; it costs one line.
lines: Cartilaginous fishes are ureotelic. They give
Bony fishes are ammonotelic. They give out
It is heterocercal in cartilaginous fishes: the
It is homocercal or diphycercal in bony fishes:
steps.why: The excretory product follows the water supply: an ammonotelic fish needs a lot of water to wash out ammonia, and a bony fish in fresh water has it.
common_mistakes: Swapping the two words. Cartilaginous fishes are ureotelic; bony fishes are ammonotelic.
Writing homocercal for the shark. Its tail lobes are unequal, so it is heterocercal.
steps.memory_tip: Cartilage: Urea, so ureotelic. Bony: ammonia. Hetero means unequal, homo means equal.

steps.label: Reproduction and examples
steps.margin_note: Finish with the examples. Two named fishes on each side complete the comparison.
lines: Present in the males of cartilaginous fishes.
Absent in the males of bony fishes.
steps.why: Claspers and viviparity go together: an animal that fertilises inside can also hold the young inside, so the last two rows are one idea.
common_mistakes: Writing that bony fishes have claspers. They are absent in the males of bony fishes.
Giving Catla as a cartilaginous fish. Catla is a bony fish; Scoliodon is the cartilaginous one.
steps.memory_tip: Claspers mean fertilisation inside, and fertilisation inside means young born alive.

insider_note: This is a comparison, so the examiner reads DOWN each column — an answer that gives five points about sharks and then three about bony fishes loses marks even when every fact is right.
